# Welcome {.unnumbered}

![](images/crew.svg){.column-body-outset .hero fig-alt="An isometric ink drawing of cartoon elephants at work around a Postgres database. One sends jobs from a laptop onto a belt, one picks a job off the belt, one carries it up a ramp into a hatch on the database, one inspects the hatch with a magnifying glass, one repairs the database with a wrench, one wheels cubes of data away, one stacks them on a pile and one checks them off on a clipboard."}

Most applications keep their rows in Postgres and add a second system as soon as they need more,
such as Redis or RabbitMQ for a queue, a separate store for vector search, or another pipeline for
change data. This book tests how much of that second system one Postgres can replace. Each chapter
gives the database one of those jobs, measures what it costs, and says where it falls short.

The measurements come from one repository, [postgres-lab](https://github.com/deburky/postgres-lab),
which runs on a laptop. Its Docker setup brings up Postgres 16 and 18 with pgvector, a replica,
PgBouncer, Apache Doris and a Postgres with pg_ducklake, next to a small FastAPI app that searches
the SQLAlchemy documentation. Every number in the text comes from one of its notebooks, and the
appendix renders each notebook with its outputs, so any claim can be checked against the run that
produced it.

## The map

![](images/world.svg){.column-body-outset .hero fig-alt="An isometric ink drawing of the book as a small world. A Postgres cylinder stands at the centre of a plate, and five districts around it stand for Python, Search, Queues, Moving data, and Access and operations."}

::: {.map}
::: {}
**Postgres from Python**

The first part connects Python to Postgres with SQLAlchemy, in both sync and async styles. It also
covers JSONB documents, PgBouncer, and PGlite, a Postgres compiled to WebAssembly that runs tests
without a server.
:::
::: {}
**Search**

The second part follows pgvector from its four distance operators to three kinds of index (HNSW,
DiskANN and PRISM), and then compares ways to load vectors in bulk.
:::
::: {}
**Queues**

The third part compares two ways to build a queue in a table. pgqueuer tracks running jobs with
heartbeats, and pgmq hides a message that is being worked on behind a visibility timeout.
:::
::: {}
**Moving data**

The fourth part streams changes from one Postgres to another with logical replication, and then
into Apache Doris with its built-in CDC. Its last chapter keeps columnar DuckLake tables inside
Postgres itself.
:::
::: {}
**Access and operations**

The fifth part writes roles and grants as code with Pulumi and pgsesame, and runs the same servers
on local Kubernetes.
:::
:::

## How to read it

Each chapter opens with what the lab measured and then explains the mechanism behind it, along with
the traps. The chapters stand alone, so they can be read in any order, and "the notebook"
in a chapter always means the one named in its last line and rendered in the appendix.

Some pages let you try things in the browser. The vector search scene in
[Chapter 1](chapters/sqlalchemy.qmd) and the queue scene in [Chapter 8](chapters/pgqueuer.qmd)
replay traces recorded from the lab's app, so the workers, the `NOTIFY`s and the HNSW searches are
real even though no server runs behind the page. Each one starts as a recording, and Run it
live opens the 3D version. The pgvector, JSONB and pgmq chapters end with a SQL console, which runs
a real Postgres inside the page.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Run it yourself

Clone the repository, then run `cp .env.example .env`, `uv sync` and `just db`. That gives you
Postgres 16 with pgvector on `localhost:5432`, and the notebooks run from there. A few need a second
server, which their chapter names. [Running the lab](chapters/running-the-lab.qmd) has the details.
:::
